summary: Provides guidelines for implementing DNS proxies such as those found in broadband gateways. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Most home routers answer your computer's DNS questions by passing them to a server run by your internet provider. This document says the router should carry those questions and answers along unchanged, so features such as DNSSEC and EDNS0 keep working.

subtitle: How a home router should relay DNS questions and answers without breaking modern DNS features.

tldr.problem: Many broadband gateways run a DNS proxy that alters or drops parts of DNS messages, which breaks features such as DNSSEC and EDNS0.
tldr.mechanism: The document sets a transparency principle, that the proxy forwards requests and responses unchanged, then lists what a conforming proxy must do about flags, record types, packet size, TCP, EDNS0, TSIG and DHCP.
tldr.outcome: Published as Best Current Practice 152 in August 2009, it is still the reference for gateway DNS proxies and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 5625 is Best Current Practice 152, published in August 2009. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the reference for how gateway DNS proxies should behave.

sections.title: Why DNS Proxies Need Rules
sections.content:
Many home routers and similar devices run a DNS proxy, a small program that receives DNS queries from devices on the local network and passes them to a resolver outside the home, usually one run by the internet service provider. The proxy normally keeps no cache of its own, so it acts as a relay rather than a full resolver.

Research cited by the document found many of these proxies incompatible with current DNS standards. It also notes that full interoperability is best achieved when a client stub resolver talks directly to a full-feature recursive resolver wherever possible. Where a client must use the gateway's proxy, the rest of the document offers guidelines to implementors.
sections.plainLanguage: Many home routers pass your DNS questions to a server at your internet provider. The document says the router should relay them unchanged, because routers that alter messages break features such as DNSSEC.

sections.title: The Transparency Principle
sections.content:
A simple proxy cannot implement every DNS feature now or in the future. The document gives the reasons: gateway hardware is limited, firmware upgrade cycles are long and many users do not apply upgrades, nobody knows what future features will look like, and supporting them would complicate the device's configuration interface. Some extensions such as EDNS0 are meant to work hop by hop, so a proxy that counts as a hop has to be fully compliant with them.

Test results cited in the document show that the more actively a proxy takes part in the DNS conversation, the more likely it is to interfere with the flow of messages. The proxy's role should therefore be no more and no less than to receive requests from clients on the LAN side, forward them verbatim to a known upstream recursive resolver on the WAN side, and ensure that the whole response is returned verbatim to the original client.

Proxies are RECOMMENDED to be as transparent as possible, so that hop-by-hop mechanisms and new extensions operate as if the proxy were not there. Except when an active security or network policy (such as a pre-authentication walled garden) requires otherwise, end users SHOULD be able to send their queries to specified upstream resolvers and bypass the proxy altogether. In that case the gateway SHOULD NOT modify the request or response packets in any way.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is simple: carry the question and the answer along exactly as written. Every extra thing a proxy does is another chance to break the message.

sections.title: Unknown Flags, Compression and Record Types
sections.content:
Combined with Postel's Robustness Principle in RFC 793, transparency means a proxy should not arbitrarily reject or drop a request or response because it looks non-compliant. Some proxies were seen dropping any packet carrying the "Authentic Data" (AD) or "Checking Disabled" (CD) bits from DNSSEC, probably because RFC 1035 originally specified that the unused "Z" flag bits MUST be zero. Those bits were always intended to be reserved for future use, so refusing such packets is not appropriate. Proxies MUST ignore any unknown DNS flags and proxy those packets as usual.

Label compression as described in Section 4.1.4 of RFC 1035 is optional, so proxies MUST forward packets regardless of the presence or absence of compressed labels. RFC 3597 requires resolvers to handle resource records of unknown type transparently, so all requests and responses MUST be proxied regardless of the values of the QTYPE and QCLASS fields, and all responses MUST be proxied regardless of the TYPE and CLASS fields of any resource record inside them.
sections.plainLanguage: If a message contains something the router has never seen before, the router should still pass it on. Refusing to handle new features breaks the systems that use them.

sections.title: Packet Size, TCP and EDNS0
sections.content:
RFC 1035 limits the DNS payload in a UDP packet to 512 octets, and a server whose answer does not fit MUST set the "TrunCation" (TC) bit in the response header. Many proxies were seen truncating every response at 512 octets, or at a size related to the WAN MTU, without correctly setting TC. Others were seen removing the TC bit from responses the server had set correctly. A truncated response with no TC bit can cause client failures, including crashes in a naive client library that reads past the data it actually received.

Since UDP packets larger than 512 octets are now expected in normal operation, proxies SHOULD NOT truncate UDP packets that exceed that size. If a proxy must unilaterally truncate a response, it MUST set the TC bit, and proxies MUST NOT remove the TC bit from responses.

The standard fail-over when a UDP query fails because of truncation is to retry over TCP, as described in Section 6.1.3.2 of RFC 1123, so DNS proxies MUST be prepared to receive and forward queries over TCP. Some "smart" proxies were seen forwarding a request that arrived over TCP onward over UDP first, only for the answer to be truncated again. A proxy that receives a request over TCP SHOULD forward it over TCP and SHOULD NOT attempt the same query over UDP first.

EDNS0 (RFC 2671) lets a client put an OPT resource record in the Additional Section of a request to advertise a receive buffer size, and that record also carries the "DNSSEC OK" (DO) flag used to ask for DNSSEC-related records. Some proxies were seen rejecting such packets with a FORMERR response code or black-holing them. Proxies MUST NOT refuse to proxy these packets.

Large UDP packets can exceed the WAN MTU, and gateways handle IP fragments in one of three ways: drop the fragments, forward each fragment as it arrives, or reassemble the packet and re-fragment it on the way out. Dropping fragments causes compatibility problems with EDNS0 unless the client advertises a buffer size limited to the WAN MTU less the size of the IP header. EDNS0 allows buffer sizes of up to 65535 octets, but most common DNS server implementations do not support a buffer size above 4096 octets, so proxies SHOULD be capable of forwarding UDP packets up to a payload size of at least 4096 octets, whichever method they use.
sections.plainLanguage: A short answer fits in one small packet. A long answer needs a bigger one, and the router has to say when it cut it short.

sections.title: Signed DNS Messages
sections.content:
TSIG (RFC 2845) is a mechanism for authenticating DNS requests and responses at the packet level. Any modification made to the DNS portions of a TSIG-signed query or response packet, other than the Query ID, causes a TSIG authentication failure.

DNS proxies MUST implement Section 4.7 of RFC 2845 and either forward packets unchanged, as recommended earlier, or fully implement TSIG. As with unknown record types, proxies MUST also be capable of proxying packets containing TKEY (RFC 2930) resource records.

The document adds a warning: any DNS proxy, such as those commonly found in WiFi hotspot walled gardens, that transparently intercepts all DNS queries and returns unsigned responses to signed queries will also cause TSIG authentication failures.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed DNS message carries proof that it is genuine. Changing even one byte of it breaks that proof, so the router must leave signed messages alone.

sections.title: How DHCP Points Clients at the Proxy
sections.content:
Most consumers rely on DHCP (RFC 2131) to obtain network configuration settings, including their IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS settings. Most gateways default to supplying their own address in the "Domain Name Server" option (Option 6, RFC 2132), so clients send their queries to the gateway's DNS proxy unless they are reconfigured. Most gateways learn their own DNS settings from values supplied by an ISP over DHCP or PPP on the WAN interface. Some gateways allow the device administrator to override those values, but others use them only for their own forwarding and do not offer them over DHCP. On such a device the only way to avoid the proxy is to hard-code the values in the client operating system, which is acceptable on a desktop but inappropriate for mobile devices that are regularly used on many different networks. Gateways are therefore RECOMMENDED to support device-administrator configuration of the "Domain Name Server" option.

For the "Domain Name" option (Option 15), a significant amount of traffic to the DNS root name servers is for invalid top-level domain names, and some of that traffic is attributed to equipment vendors whose firmware defaults this option to specific values. Since no standard exists for a local scoped domain name suffix, it is RECOMMENDED that the default value for this option be empty, and that the option MUST NOT be sent to clients when no value is configured.

Lease timing matters too. If the DHCP lease is obtained while the WAN link is down, the client keeps the gateway's own address until the lease is renewed. The document offers no firm rule but suggests giving consideration to lease length, to forcing a renewal, to persisting learned upstream values in non-volatile memory (with the risk of offering incorrect values if the device is moved or connected to another ISP), or to issuing only very short leases of 60 seconds while the WAN link is down. With that last approach, the document notes, a DNS proxy might not be needed at all.
sections.plainLanguage: When your device joins the network, the router tells it which DNS server to use. The router should let its owner change that answer, and it should not hand out invented domain names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document introduces no new protocols, but it lists security-related recommendations for vendors. Many proxies pick a new Query ID for outbound requests so that responses are directed to the correct client. Changing the Query ID is acceptable and compatible with proxying TSIG-signed packets, because the TSIG signature calculation is based on the original message ID carried in the TSIG record. However, many proxies were seen picking sequential Query IDs for successive requests. Proxies are strongly RECOMMENDED to follow the relevant recommendations in RFC 5452, particularly Section 9.2 on randomisation of Query IDs and source ports, and this also applies to source port selection within any NAT function. A proxy on a gateway with NAT compliant with RFC 4787 SHOULD also follow Section 10 of RFC 5452 on how long DNS state is kept.

Some gateways have their DNS proxy listening on both internal (LAN) and external (WAN) interfaces. In that configuration the proxy can be used to mount reflector attacks as described in RFC 5358. The DNS proxy in a gateway SHOULD NOT, by default, be accessible from the WAN interfaces of the device.

Deep packet inspection sits uneasily with transparency, but the document separates traffic that is intrinsically malformed from traffic that merely contains unexpected data. Packets that MAY be dropped include those with invalid compression pointers, meaning pointers that point outside the current packet or that might cause a parsing loop, and those with incorrect counts for the Question, Answer, Authority and Additional sections, though care is needed where truncation is possible. Dropped packets cause the client to repeatedly retransmit the original request and detect the error only after several retransmit intervals, so proxies SHOULD synthesise a suitable DNS error response to the client, such as SERVFAIL, instead of dropping the packet completely.
sections.plainLanguage: The router should not use easy-to-guess ticket numbers, should serve only people inside the house, and should report an error rather than stay silent when a packet is broken.
